questions.stem: An engineer asks: "Which classes extend `BasePaymentHandler`?" The codebase is 2 million lines across Java and Python, with no naming convention for handler files. Which built-in tool should the agent use first?

options.text: Glob with `**/*Handler*` to list candidate files by name, then Read each candidate to confirm whether it extends the base class.
options.why: Glob matches paths. Subclasses may have any file name, so this misses some and wastes reads on others.

options.text: Grep for a pattern such as `extends BasePaymentHandler` (and the Python equivalent) across the codebase.
options.why: Grep searches inside files, which is what this question needs.

options.text: Bash with `find . -name '*.java' | xargs cat`, so the agent can scan the complete source for the base class name.
options.why: This floods the context with the entire codebase.

options.text: Read the `BasePaymentHandler` source file first, since base classes usually document their known subclasses.
options.why: That is an unreliable assumption. A content search answers the question directly.

questions.explanation: Grep searches file contents. Glob matches file paths and names.

questions.stem: The agent needs a list of every Terraform file under any `modules/` directory, at any depth, to check which ones still use a deprecated provider. Which built-in tool should it use to build that list?

options.text: Grep for the string `provider` in all files, and keep only the paths that contain `modules/` in the results.
options.why: This misses Terraform files that don't mention `provider`, and it includes non-Terraform matches.

options.text: Read the root `main.tf`, and follow its module source references recursively to discover every module file.
options.why: This misses unreferenced modules and is slow and error-prone.

options.text: Glob with the pattern `**/modules/**/*.tf`.
options.why: Matching path patterns is what Glob is for.

options.text: Bash with `ls -R modules/`, then filter the listing for files that end in `.tf`.
options.why: This only covers a top-level `modules/` directory and is a clumsy substitute for Glob.

questions.explanation: Use Glob to match path patterns and Grep to search content. The two can then be combined.

questions.stem: The agent's Edit call fails because the `old_string` it chose (`return null;`) appears 14 times in the file. It only needs to change the occurrence inside `findAccountById`. What should it do?

options.text: Retry Edit with a longer anchor that includes surrounding lines, making it unique. If that isn't feasible, fall back to Read and Write.
options.why: Edit needs a unique match, and Read + Write is the fallback.

options.text: Use Edit with replace-all, since `return undefined;` is equivalent in most call sites and the tests will catch any difference.
options.why: That changes 13 occurrences that shouldn't change.

options.text: Use Bash with `sed -i` and a line-number address, after finding the line with Grep, to change only that line.
options.why: This is fragile if line numbers shift, and it bypasses the safer edit tooling.

options.text: Report the failure to the engineer and ask them to make that one change by hand, since the anchor isn't unique.
options.why: There is a standard recovery path, so giving up is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Edit requires unique anchor text. Widen the context to make it unique, or fall back to Read + Write.

questions.stem: A wiki MCP server is connected, but for questions like "what's our on-call escalation policy?" the agent keeps running Grep over the repo, finds nothing, and answers vaguely. The policy is documented only in the wiki. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools, so it is forced to use the wiki for any question it can't answer directly.
options.why: Grep is essential for the code questions that make up most of the traffic.

options.text: Mirror the wiki's policy pages into a `docs/` folder in the repo nightly, so that Grep can find them.
options.why: This duplicates the source of truth, and the copies go stale.

options.text: Force the wiki tool with `tool_choice` whenever the question contains words like "policy" or "process".
options.why: Keyword routing is brittle and bypasses the model's judgement.

options.text: Rewrite the wiki tool's description to say it searches internal policies, runbooks and process docs absent from the repo, with examples.
options.why: Weak MCP tool descriptions lose to familiar built-in tools. Clear descriptions fix the selection.

questions.explanation: Enhance MCP tool descriptions so the agent picks them over built-in tools when appropriate.

questions.stem: The team needs the agent to read GitHub issues and post comments on them. A developer proposes writing a custom MCP server against the GitHub API, which they estimate at two weeks of work. What is the better first option?

options.text: Use an established GitHub MCP server, and build custom tools only for Halyard-specific gaps.
options.why: Prefer existing servers for standard integrations. Custom servers add maintenance burden.

options.text: Build the custom server, since owning the code allows the tool descriptions to be tuned precisely for this agent.
options.why: This incurs build and maintenance cost for a standard integration. Descriptions can be improved without owning the server.

options.text: Give the agent Bash access with a GitHub token in its environment, and let it call the REST API with `curl`.
options.why: This is less safe and less structured, and the agent handles auth and pagination ad hoc.

options.text: Export issues nightly into the internal wiki, so the agent can read them through the existing wiki MCP server.
options.why: The data goes stale, and the agent still can't post comments.

questions.explanation: For standard integrations, prefer community or official MCP servers over building custom ones.

questions.stem: An engineer adds a new MCP server to the project's `.mcp.json` while an agent session is running. They then ask the agent to use it, but the agent says no such tools exist. Why?

options.text: Servers in `.mcp.json` need approving with `/permissions` before their tools are shown to the agent.
options.why: Approval prompts may exist, but the core issue is when tools are discovered.

options.text: Tools are discovered when the client connects to the servers, so the session must reconnect or restart to see the new one.
options.why: Tool discovery happens at connection time.

options.text: MCP servers can only be configured at user scope (`~/.claude.json`), so project-scope entries are silently ignored.
options.why: Project scope through `.mcp.json` is supported.

options.text: New tools are only offered once the agent's `tool_choice` is set to `any`, which tells it to look for additional tools.
options.why: `tool_choice` controls whether tools are called, not which tools are discovered.

questions.explanation: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time.

questions.stem: The `legacy/billing/` tree has conventions that differ from the rest of the codebase: Java 8, no Lombok, and a custom logging wrapper. Engineers working there use Claude Code too. Where should those conventions live?

options.text: In the root CLAUDE.md under a "Legacy billing" heading, so they are always available whenever someone works on billing.
options.why: They would bloat every session and risk being applied elsewhere.

options.text: In a `.claude/rules/billing.md` file whose `paths:` glob matches every Java file in the repository.
options.why: That glob is far too broad. It would load the rules for non-billing Java code too.

options.text: In a CLAUDE.md inside `legacy/billing/`, which applies when working in that directory tree.
options.why: Directory-level memory suits conventions that follow the directory tree.

options.text: In a `/billing-conventions` skill that engineers are told to invoke before they edit billing code.
options.why: The conventions wouldn't apply automatically.

questions.explanation: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md suits conventions bounded by a directory. Path-glob rules suit scattered files, but only with a correctly scoped glob.

questions.stem: The deployment runbook is 400 lines and is needed in perhaps 5% of sessions. One engineer wants to paste it into CLAUDE.md, and another wants to make it a skill. What is the deciding difference?

options.text: Skills can't include long reference material, so CLAUDE.md is the only place a 400-line runbook can live.
options.why: Skills can bundle reference files. This statement is false.

options.text: CLAUDE.md content is only read in plan mode, so a skill is the only way to use the runbook during execution.
options.why: False. CLAUDE.md loads in every mode.

options.text: Skills are personal by default and can't be shared, so the runbook has to go in CLAUDE.md to reach the team.
options.why: Project skills in `.claude/skills/` are shared through the repo.

options.text: A skill loads on demand when relevant. CLAUDE.md loads into every session, costing context the other 95% of the time.
options.why: This is the essential trade-off between on-demand and always-on context.

questions.explanation: Use CLAUDE.md for what must always apply and skills for specialised procedures that load on demand.

questions.stem: A `/db-migrate` skill should only read files and run the migration CLI (`./bin/migrate`). Security requires that it can never edit source code, even if a user asks it to mid-run. Which mechanism enforces this?

options.text: Set `context: fork` in the frontmatter, so the skill runs isolated and can't modify the caller's files.
options.why: A forked context isolates the conversation, not filesystem access.

options.text: List only the permitted tools in `allowed-tools` (Read and the specific Bash migrate command).
options.why: This restricts the skill's tool access structurally.

options.text: Put a prominent "Never edit files" rule at the top of SKILL.md, followed by an explanation of the security requirement.
options.why: This is probabilistic. A user request mid-run could override it.

options.text: Add an `argument-hint` of `<migration-name>`, so the skill only accepts a migration name and nothing else.
options.why: This documents the arguments. It restricts nothing.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter restricts which tools a skill may use, which follows least privilege.

questions.stem: An engineer has three review comments on Claude's patch: (1) rename `fetchAcct` to `fetchAccount`; (2) change the interface that `fetchAccount` implements, in the same module; (3) fix an unrelated typo in the README. How should the feedback be delivered?

options.text: Send (1) and (2) together, since they interact, and handle (3) separately.
options.why: Batch interacting issues together and handle independent ones sequentially.

options.text: Send each comment in its own message, in order, waiting for Claude to finish each before sending the next.
options.why: Splitting interacting changes risks inconsistent intermediate states between (1) and (2).

options.text: Send all three in one message, so Claude can plan the changes together and avoid repeated test runs.
options.why: Mixing an unrelated fix into an interdependent change dilutes focus and complicates review.

options.text: Send (3) first because it's quickest, then (2), then (1), so the riskiest change is made with the most context.
options.why: This order separates the two interacting changes and has no real benefit.

questions.explanation: Iterative refinement means grouping interdependent changes and sequencing independent ones.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Claude to build an internal CLI for rotating service credentials. They only have a vague idea of the requirements and admit they "haven't thought about edge cases". Which technique is most likely to produce the right tool?

options.text: Ask Claude to build the most complete version it can, covering every edge case it can think of, then trim the unused features.
options.why: This produces a bloated tool that is still built on guessed requirements.

options.text: Have Claude write a first version immediately, and refine it based on whatever problems come up in real use.
options.why: This is risky for credential tooling, and it wastes iterations on the wrong problem.

options.text: Use the interview pattern: have Claude ask about requirements, constraints and edge cases before any code is written.
options.why: It surfaces requirements that the engineer hasn't articulated.

options.text: Ask Claude to find an open-source credential rotation tool and adapt it to the internal environment.
options.why: This may help later, but the requirements still haven't been established.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern is a refinement technique for underspecified tasks.

questions.stem: An engineer asks: "Find every place we handle currency rounding and check they're consistent." Rounding logic is spread across about 300 files in four services and two languages. What is the best decomposition?

options.text: Load all candidate files into one large prompt, so the model can compare every implementation side by side.
options.why: Attention dilutes over huge inputs, and the context limit is likely exceeded.

options.text: Sample the 20 most-modified files from git history, on the theory that inconsistencies concentrate in frequently changed code.
options.why: This leaves coverage gaps on an explicit "find every place" request.

options.text: Ask each service's owning team to list their rounding call sites, then have Claude compare the lists.
options.why: The agent can map the call sites itself. This is slow and incomplete.

options.text: Map the call sites with Grep, analyse each file or module in focused passes, then compare approaches in a cross-file pass.
options.why: Local passes plus an integration pass avoid attention dilution.

questions.explanation: For broad analysis, map the structure, do per-file local passes, then run an integration pass across files.

questions.stem: A few sessions per week enter runaway loops of more than 200 tool calls, which burns budget. The developer wants a safety mechanism without breaking the legitimate long tasks, some of which take about 60 calls. What approach is correct?

options.text: Replace `stop_reason` handling with a hard cap of 25 iterations, which covers the typical task and prevents runaways.
options.why: This truncates the legitimate 60-call tasks. Using a cap as the primary stop is an anti-pattern.

options.text: Keep `stop_reason` as the stop signal, and add a generous budget cap only as a backstop that escalates when hit.
options.why: Caps are acceptable as a backstop, not as the primary termination mechanism.

options.text: Ask the model to report its progress every ten calls, and stop the loop if the report says it is stuck.
options.why: This relies on parsing self-reported natural language.

options.text: Remove Bash after 50 calls, since runaway loops are usually repeated shell commands, and let other tools continue.
options.why: This is arbitrary and breaks legitimate tasks without addressing the cause.

questions.explanation: Loop control relies on `stop_reason`. Limits are only safety nets with explicit handling.

questions.stem: The assistant has Bash access in environments connected to staging clusters. It must never run `kubectl delete` or `terraform destroy`, even if an engineer's prompt asks it to, or if text pulled from a ticket tells it to. What is the most reliable control?

options.text: A system-prompt rule to refuse destructive commands, reinforced with examples of refusing them politely.
options.why: This is probabilistic, and it can be overridden by user pressure or prompt injection.

options.text: Require the assistant to explain each Bash command's effect before running it, and to skip anything it calls destructive.
options.why: The guarantee still depends on the model's own judgement.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook or deny rule that blocks those command patterns in Bash and returns an explanation.
options.why: Destructive actions need deterministic, code-level enforcement.

options.text: Log every Bash command to a SIEM, and alert the security team whenever a destructive pattern is detected.
options.why: This detects the damage after it has happened. It is useful as an addition, not as the control.

questions.explanation: Use hooks and permission rules for hard guarantees. Prompts can only guide.

questions.stem: Engineers ask questions spanning code, the issue tracker and deployment history. A developer proposes three specialised subagents behind a coordinator, instead of the current single agent with all the tools. When is the multi-agent design the better choice?

options.text: When each area generates verbose intermediate work and needs its own tools; subagents then isolate context and return concise findings.
options.why: Context isolation and focused toolsets are the main benefits of subagents.

options.text: Always: splitting work across more agents reliably improves answer quality, regardless of how complex the questions are.
options.why: Multi-agent systems add latency and cost. They aren't always better.

options.text: Only when the three areas are served by different MCP servers, because one agent can't hold tools from several servers.
options.why: One agent can use tools from many servers.

options.text: When questions are short and simple, since subagents are faster than a single agent with a large toolset.
options.why: Simple questions are where the coordination overhead is least worth it.

questions.explanation: Choose multi-agent designs for context isolation, parallelism and scoped tools, not by default.

questions.stem: In a three-hour debugging session, the assistant has piled up many large Bash outputs and file reads. It is now contradicting conclusions it confirmed earlier. Which TWO actions help most? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Write the confirmed findings to a scratchpad file, and refer to it instead of the raw outputs.
options.why: Durable, compact notes beat a long, noisy history.

options.text: Compact the conversation, or start a new session seeded with a summary of the confirmed findings.
options.why: This resets the degraded context while keeping the essentials.

options.text: Re-run the key diagnostic commands, so their outputs are recent and closer to the end of the context.
options.why: This adds even more bloat.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` on each response, so the assistant can restate its full reasoning in every reply.
options.why: That affects output length, not the quality of the context.

options.text: Turn on extended thinking for every turn, so the assistant can reconcile the contradictions itself.
options.why: This doesn't remove the bloated context that is causing the problem.

questions.explanation: Context degradation in long sessions is countered with scratchpads, compaction or summarisation, and fresh contexts.
